'''''Hypericum majus''''', the '''greater Canadian St. John's wort''', is a perennial herb native to North America. The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific epithet]] ''majus'' means "larger". The plant has a [[diploid number]] of 16.

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Hypericum majus BB-1913.png|thumb|Illustration from ''An Illustrated Flora of the Northern United States'']]
''Hypericum majus'' is a more northern relative of ''[[Hypericum pauciflorum]]''. ''H. majus'' differs from its relative in its annual habit, thinner leaves, smaller flowers, and doubly branching inflorescence. In the past the species was the western part of a [[vicariant]] species including the more eastern ''[[Hypericum canadense]]''. The two species became [[sympatric]] when north-eastern North America became [[glaciated]] and the two now hybridize, most notably in Wisconsin. Hybrids of the two species are shorter than ''H. majus'' and have leaves of intermediate length, width, and vein number.<ref name=Bulletin/> ''H. majus'' also hybridizes with [[Hypericum mutilum|''Hypericum mutilum'' subsp. ''mutilum'']] in Maine and with [[Hypericum mutilum|''Hypericum mutilum'' subsp. ''boreale'']] in Wisconsin and Michigan. The hybrid of latter can be distinguished by its intermediate [[seed capsule]] shape, similar to [[Hypericum × dissimulatum|''H.'' × ''dissimulatum'']] though with more broad leaves.<ref>{{cite book |page= [https://archive.org/details/newenglandwildfl0000hain/page/626 626] |title= New England Wild Flower Society's Flora Novae Angliae: A Manual for the Identification of Native and Naturalized Higher Vascular Plants of New England |url= https://archive.org/details/newenglandwildfl0000hain |url-access= registration |author= Arthur Haines |edition= illustrated |publisher= Yale University Press |year= 2011 |isbn= 9780300171549}}</ref>

==Description==

''Hypericum majus'' is a perennial bearing short leafy shoots with solitary or tufted stems. The erect and stout herb grows {{convert|10-70|cm|abbr=on}} tall and has a [[taproot]]. The roots are fibrous and lack [[rhizome]]s or runners but can grow short offshoots in autumn. The four-angled, squarish, green stems can become [[wikt:ancipitous|ancipitous]]. The stems tend to branch more in the upper half of the plant but branches can grow from the lower half when the terminal [[meristem]] is damaged. The [[Internode (botany)|internode]]s are {{convert|1-4|cm|abbr=on}}, the upper of which can exceed the leaves. The simple or opposite, [[lanceolate]] leaves are {{convert|1.5-4.5|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|5-15|mm|abbr=on}} wide.  Leaves are erect or spreading, planar, and [[Glossary of botanical terms#chartaceous|chartaceous]]. The leaves have acute to rounded apices, cuneate bases, and an entire margin. The upper leaves have five to seven veins arising from their rounded, [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or clasping base. The basal leaves are more purplish and crowded, and measure {{convert|4-5|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2-3|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The tertiary reticulation is dense as are the laminar glands that create the punctiform pattern. The terminal [[inflorescence]] is three to thirty flowered. The branching of the inflorescence is mostly [[dichasium|dichasial]], with ascending pairs of flowering branches rising five nodes below. The entire inflorescence is [[corymb]]iform to cylindric, though in smaller plants the inflorescence is a simple, nearly naked [[Cyme (botany)|cyme]]. The cymes are subtended by slender [[bract]]s measuring {{convert|3-4|mm|abbr=on}} long. [[Pedicel (botany)|Pedicel]]s are {{convert|3-5|mm|abbr=on}} long and the star-shaped flowers are {{convert|6-7|mm|abbr=on}} wide, with the central flower being the largest. The sepals are [[Glossary of botanical terms#attenuate|lance-attenuate]], measuring {{convert|4-7|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.8-1.5|mm|abbr=on}} wide. Two sepals are typically longer and wider than the other three. Sepals have three to five veins, with a visible midvein, and lack the punctiform glands. The golden yellow, occasionally tinged pink petals are {{convert|3.5-6|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.25-1.75|mm|abbr=on}} wide, equal or shorter than the sepals. The twelve to twenty-one [[stamen]]s are obscurely five-[[Fascicle (botany)|fascicle]]d, the longest measuring {{convert|2.5-3.5|mm|abbr=on}}. The sessile [[pistil]] is about {{convert|3|mm|abbr=on}} long, ovoid in shape. The ovoid to ellipsoid [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is {{convert|1.5-2|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.8-1|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The three [[carpel]]s are at first distinct and become indistinct.<ref name=Canada>{{cite journal |page= 17 |title= The St. John's-worts of Canada (Guttiferae) |last1= Gillett |first1= John Montague |last2= Robson |first2= Norman Keith Bonner |journal= The St. John's-worts of Canada (Guttiferae) |number= 11 |year= 1981 |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/178727#page/23/mode/1up |publisher= National Museums of Canada}}</ref> The three [[Style (botany)|style]]s are {{convert|0.6-1|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[seed capsule|capsule]] is conic-ellipsoid, measuring {{convert|4-8|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2.5-3.5|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The seeds are {{convert|0.5-0.7|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Manual>{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author= Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year= 1970 |editor= R. C. Rollins |publisher= D. Van Nostrand Company |edition= Eighth (Centennial) - Illustrated|isbn= 0-442-22250-5 |page= 1013}}</ref><ref name=Bulletin>{{cite book |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/19494#page/109/mode/1up |page= 108 |title= Studies in the genus Hypericum L. (Guttiferae) 8. Sections 29. Brathys (part 2) and 30. Trigynobrathys |series= Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History). |volume= 1 |publisher= British Museum (Natural History) |author= Norman K. B. Robson |year= 1951}}</ref>

''H. majus'' can be distinguished from other small-flowered ''Hypericum'' species by its leaves with five to seven veins.<ref>{{cite book |page= 326 |title= Acanthaceae to Myricaceae: Water Willows to Wax Myrtles |series= Aquatic and Standing Water Plants |volume= 3 |author= Robert H. Mohlenbrock |edition= illustrated, revised |publisher= SIU Press |year= 2008 |isbn= 9780809327904}}</ref>

The herb flowers from June to September.<ref>{{cite book |page= 535 |title= An Illustrated Flora of the Northern United States, Canada and the British Possessions: From Newfoundland to the Parallel of the Southern Boundary of Virginia, and from the Atlantic Ocean Westward to the 102d Meridian |volume= 2 |author= Nathaniel Lord Britton, Addison Brown |edition= 2 |publisher= Charles Scribner's Sons |year= 1913}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==

''Hypericum majus'' grows in wet or dry open soil in bogs, marshes, ditches, meadows, woodlands, and other damp habitats.<ref name=Manual/> It prefers elevations between {{convert|0-1200|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name=Bulletin/>

The herb occurs in [[New Brunswick]] and [[Quebec]] to southern [[British Columbia]]. To the south it is distributed from [[Maine]] to [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and as far south as [[Colorado]], [[Kansas]], and [[Ohio]].<ref name=Manual/> It was introduced into [[France]] by 1955, into [[Germany]] by 1948, and into [[Japan]] by 1974, though the method of introduction is unknown.<ref name=Bulletin/>
